newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvians frustrated with hostage crisis handling.
newsitem.headline: Peruvians frustrated with hostage crisis handling.

text.p: Peruvians have grown frustrated with the way the 110-day-old hostage crisis is being handled, but they support President Alberto Fujimori's pledge to reach a negotiated solution, an opinion poll showed on Sunday.

The poll, conducted by consulting firm CPI and published in the local newspaper El Comercio, showed that approval for Fujimori's management of the siege at the Japanese ambassador's house had fallen to 28 percent from 66 percent in January.

The survey results reflected impatience with the slow pace of talks to free the 72 hostages held by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels. Twenty percent of respondents said the government should give more ground to win a solution and 49 percent said the MRTA should do so.

MRTA rebels stormed the house during a cocktail party on Dec. 17, 1996, and took more than 500 guests hostage. They released most of the hostages, but kept a group including two cabinet ministers, Fujimori's brother and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.
Fujimori on Saturday renewed his pledge to find a negotiated settlement to the crisis, saying he would intervene with force only as a last resort in an "uncontrollable emergency."
"We will continue exhausting all efforts ... to reach a peaceful outcome," Fujimori said during a news conference in the Bolivian city of Santa Cruz.
Fujimori's tough negotiating stance was backed on Sunday by two U.S. security experts during a discussion on the Cable New Network's Spanish language channel.

"We have to send a clear message to terrorists, rebels, criminals or guerrillas that the tactic of hostage-taking is wrong and does not work," said Michael Skol, a former State Department assistant secretary.
"There should be no concessions and one has to be prepared for a military action," said independent security expert William Perry.
A majority of Peruvians believe a negotiated solution should be sought. Eighty-one percent said Fujimori should not use force to free the hostages, up from 76 percent in March.

Fujimori's overall approval rating was steady at 50 percent, unchanged from January, according to the poll of 400 people in Lima and the neighbouring city of Callao. The poll did not give a margin of error.
With talks reported to be languishing, speculation was rife in Lima that one of the crisis mediators had taken negotiations directly to the hostage-takers' leadership.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a member of a three-man mediation team, visited a naval base in the port of Callao where the MRTA's maximum leader Victor Polay and at least two other MRTA prisoners are serving life sentences.

News reports said Cipriani spoke to Polay during the hour- long visit to the prison on Friday evening. Cipriani was silent about the visit, but early on Sunday, MRTA made a reference to the base in two new posters it hung from a residence window.

One poster said, "Down with the jail-tombs of the Callao naval base," and another saluted Polay on his 44th birthday on Sunday: "MRTA Commander Victor Polay, we salute you on your day. Your resistance and courage are an example for everyone."
Local newspapers speculated that Cipriani hoped Polay would persuade Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, leader of the MRTA guerrillas holed up in the diplomatic compound, to give up his struggle.

Cipriani visited the residence for about two hours on Sunday before meeting with fellow mediators Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig. Vincent later left for Bolivia where he said he would be attending to diplomatic duties unconnected with the hostage crisis.
Fujimori's government has not met the hostage-takers for face-to-face talks since mid-March, leaving the mediation panel to carry out a kind of shuttle diplomacy between the two sides.
